newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia Probanka sees custodian accounts in May.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia Probanka sees custodian accounts in May.

text.p: Slovenian bank Probanka said on Wednesday it expected to open its first custodian accounts for international portfolio investors in early May.

"We expect the first account contracts will be signed in the first half of May and trading through them is expected to start immediately after that," Milana Lah, Probanka's global finance director, told Reuters.
In February the Bank of Slovenia blocked foreign buying, stipulating international investors must open custodian accounts at any of Slovenia's 14 fully licensed banks in order to trade in securities.
Since then the blue-chip SBI index has fallen by 21 percent, while average daily volume has dropped to about 50 million tolars ($0.3 million) from 500 million previously.
Probanka said the costs of the accounts would be 8.9 percent of the amount handled, and that the bank would be able to accept an inflow of five million marks ($2.9 million) immediately.
Banks SKB, Vipa, Creditanstalt, Bank Austria and Nova Ljubljanska Banka said they had prepared custodian account schemes but it could take over a month before the first contracts were signed.

"As expected international investors are taking time to consider the offer mainly because of the costs, as the costs of similar accounts in Western European countries are about half," said Alenka Markovic, director of SKB's securities department.
SKB said the costs of the accounts would be about nine percent, while other banks estimated the costs would be between 10 to 15 percent.

Banks said high costs were a result of the Bank of Slovenia regulations, according to which banks have to consider the money paid into the accounts as liabilities which they must balance against assets.
Market participants said the SBI index could jump by about 10 percent immediately after the opening of the first accounts, but warned the rise might be short-lived.
"Most foreign investors consider the costs of the accounts to be too high therefore even when the accounts are open the inflow of foreign capital may be poor," a trader said.

"Although some people are interested in Slovenian securities they worry about the cost of investing, therefore the market may be stuck with very little foreign participation for months," a London-based investor said.

He said most international investors consider pharmaceutical firms Lek and Krka and food makers Droga and Kolinska to be the most attractive Slovenian shares. -- Marja Novak, Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
